entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sextus Propertius (c. 50–45 BCE – c. 15 BCE) was a preeminent Roman elegiac poet of the Augustan age, whose four books of *Elegies* profoundly shaped the course of Latin love poetry and established him as a canonical voice alongside Catullus and Tibullus. Born in Assisium (modern Assisi), Umbria, he rose to prominence within the literary circle of Maecenas, Augustus's influential patron of the arts, navigating the complex political and cultural landscape of Rome's transition from Republic to Empire. His work, deeply personal yet politically aware, offers an intimate window into the emotional and social currents of late 1st century BCE Roman society, especially the idealized, often tumultuous, relationship with his beloved 'Cynthia'.

Propertius's poetic output, primarily composed between 29 and 16 BCE, consists of four books of *Elegies* totaling approximately 3,500 lines. These poems largely revolve around his passionate, frequently agonizing, affair with a woman he calls Cynthia, whose real identity is believed to be Hostia. Beyond the intense personal drama, Propertius's later works, particularly Book IV, expanded the scope of elegy to include aetiological themes, exploring the origins of Roman rituals, myths, and place names (e.g., 'The Temple of Apollo on the Palatine'). This innovative blend of personal emotion and national myth distinguished his work, demonstrating his mastery of the elegiac couplet and his sophisticated engagement with Hellenistic literary traditions, particularly Callimachus.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Propertius significantly shaped the elegiac genre in Latin literature, influencing subsequent poets like Ovid and contributing to the enduring tradition of European love poetry. His work provides invaluable insight into the personal and cultural landscape of the Augustan Age.
